p: Mir Osman Ali Khan was born on 5 or 6 April 1886 at Purani Haveli, the second son of Mahboob Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, and Amat-uz-Zahra Begum. He was educated privately and reportedly became fluent in Urdu, Persian, Arabic and English; from early 1899 Brian Egerton served for two years as his English tutor. His father died on 29 August 1911, and he was proclaimed Nizam the same day; the coronation was held at the Chowmahalla Palace on 18 September 1911. He lived at King Kothi Palace from the age of 13 until his death.

Hyderabad was the largest of the princely states of colonial India, and its ruler was one of only five princes entitled to a 21-gun salute. For his financial contribution to the British war effort in the First World War, amounting to nearly £25 million, King George V raised his style in 1918 to His Exalted Highness, and he was named Faithful Ally of the British Government. After the Great Musi Flood of 1908 he had two reservoirs, Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar, built on the advice of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. In 1919 he formed an Executive Council, and in 1941 the Hyderabad State Bank, which managed the state's own currency.

When the British withdrew in 1947 the Nizam ruled more than 16 million people. He refused to sign the instrument of accession, preferring a separate kingdom within the British Commonwealth, and signed a one-year standstill agreement instead. He negotiated openly with India and covertly with Pakistan, while his power was weakened by the Telangana Rebellion and by the Razakars, a Muslim militia he could not put down. In 1948 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Polo, under Major General Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri, and the annexation was over in 109 hours. The Nizam kept his personal wealth and title.

He served as Rajpramukh of Hyderabad State from 26 January 1950 to 31 October 1956, after which the state was partitioned. He gave 14,000 acres of his estate to the Bhoodan movement of Vinoba Bhave for distribution among landless farmers. He died on 24 February 1967 and was buried the next day, as his will asked, in the Masjid-e Judi, where his mother lay; the chief curator of the Nizam's Museum, D. Bhaskara Rao, put the funeral procession at an estimated one million people. His grandson Mukarram Jah succeeded him as titular Nizam.

notes: The article gives the state's area twice, differently (86,000 and 82,698 square miles); left out.

Wealth figures conflict throughout (US$2 billion in the early 1940s; Rs 660 crore; £110 million; 2% of US GDP); I gave none, since the description already says he was reputed the richest man in the world.

The article says that in October 1962 'the PM Lal Bahadur Shastri' asked him for gold for the National Defence Fund and he gave 5,000 kilos; the date and the office do not seem to fit together, so I left the whole item out.
The article says both that he wanted independence 'or to join Pakistan' (lead) and that he 'refused to join either' (body). I used the body's wording.
'Titular Nizam' renders the article's 'de jure Nizam' for Mukarram Jah.
The article gives the Musi flood's dead as 'thousands' in one place and 'an estimated 50,000' in another; left out.
